correctness.rationale: On an SPD quadratic, a nonterminal ball step is y=(I+sH)^(-1)x with s>0. Within each occupied dyadic eigenband the coordinate decrement factors have ratio less than two, so band displacement is at most twice the band-norm decrease. Telescoping and Cauchy-Schwarz prove 2 sqrt(p) D, while sign-preserving coordinate monotonicity proves sqrt(d) D. Each nonterminal fixed-radius movement has length h, establishing finite-call complexity. Geometrically spaced eigenvalues and disjoint gradient-flow time intervals give (exp(-1/2)-exp(-1))sqrt(p) arclength; on every compact nonzero segment the backward-Euler recurrence converges to the normalized gradient-flow curve, transferring the lower bound to liminf h N_h. The standalone checker passed 80671 finite checks; proof does not depend on finite enumeration.

originality.rationale: The established implicit ball-proximal step and the known quadratic gradient-flow square-root-log path-length phenomenon are credited. The accepted new mathematical implication is a uniform, nonasymptotic, arbitrary-radius length estimate for a different implicit variable-resolvent algorithm, the resulting fixed-radius finite-call bound, and a matching lower-order transfer. Searches and paper-section comparisons found no stronger coverage, subject to unindexed-source risk.
residual_risks: An unindexed implicit-proximal or quadratic trust-region path-length theorem may already cover the statement.
The sharp-order ordinary gradient-flow result is prior work; originality is limited to its nonasymptotic arbitrary-radius ball-proximal transfer.

value.rationale: A general exact ball-proximal method has a dimension-dependent linear termination bound and a potentially quadratic dimension-free bound. For the motivated SPD quadratic subclass, the new theorem supplies a radius-schedule-independent length certificate with only square-root logarithmic condition-number dependence, plus a sharp-order geometric-spectrum family. This provides a reusable ideal-oracle numerical-optimization benchmark distinct from previously known gradient-flow results, without claiming practical speedup or exact optimal constants.
